content: 1. Approximately 7 million individuals are newly infected with HIV each year, highlighting the urgent need for more effective prevention strategies. Oral antiretroviral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) has emerged as a promising tool for preventing HIV transmission, particularly among high-risk populations. 2. The objective of the study was to assess the efficacy of oral antiretroviral chemoprophylaxis in preventing HIV infection among HIV-negative individuals at high risk of exposure. 3. A systematic search was conducted in April 2012 using databases such as MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and EMBASE, along with clinical trial registries, to identify relevant studies. 4. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials evaluating the effects of any antiretroviral agent or combination of agents in preventing HIV infection in high-risk populations. 5. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors using a standardized form, and relative risk with a 95% confidence interval was used as the measure of effect. 6. Twelve randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria, with six studies providing data for the review, encompassing a total of 9,849 participants. These trials evaluated daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) plus emtricitabine (FTC) versus placebo, TDF alone versus placebo, and daily TDF-FTC versus intermittent TDF-FTC. 7. One trial included three study arms: TDF, TDF-FTC, and placebo. No significant differences in adverse event risks were observed across the studies, and adherence and sexual behaviors were similar between intervention and control groups. 8. The findings suggest that pre-exposure prophylaxis with TDF alone or in combination with FTC significantly reduces the risk of acquiring HIV in high-risk populations, including individuals in serodiscordant relationships, men who have sex with men (MSM), and other high-risk men and women. 9. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the use of tenofovir-emtricitabine for PrEP, and its cost-effectiveness has been evaluated in both the United States and South Africa. PrEP was found to be cost-effective in high-risk MSM with an HIV incidence of at least 2% in the U.S. and in young women in South Africa, depending on cost and efficacy assumptions. 10. Future cost-effectiveness studies should address implementation issues such as uptake in high-risk versus low-risk groups, duration of PrEP use, adherence, budget impact, and the role of PrEP as part of combination HIV prevention strategies, including expanded testing and treatment access. 11. Research on the acceptability of oral PrEP and treatment as prevention (TasP) has primarily focused on MSM in the U.S., with limited data on other populations. Key research gaps include understanding TasP acceptability among people living with HIV, motivations for PrEP use and adherence, risk perceptions, social and structural factors, and consistent definitions of acceptability. 12. Mathematical modeling studies have demonstrated that PrEP can be a cost-effective addition to HIV prevention programs when targeted to key populations at highest risk of HIV exposure. However, its effectiveness depends on program characteristics such as coverage, prioritization strategies, and adherence. 13. PrEP alone will not eliminate HIV transmission due to its incomplete efficacy, reliance on adherence, and high program costs, which may limit achievable coverage levels. Strategic implementation targeting key populations is essential for maximizing its impact. 14. In the U.S., initiating PrEP in 20% of MSM could reduce new HIV infections by 13% over 20 years, with a cost of $172,091 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. Expanding coverage to all MSM would prevent more infections but at a higher cost per QALY. 15. PrEP is most cost-effective when provided to high-risk MSM, with costs approximating $50,000 per QALY gained. However, providing PrEP to all high-risk MSM for 20 years would result in substantial healthcare expenditures, highlighting the need for targeted implementation. 16. Sensitivity analyses indicate that PrEP costs less than $100,000 per QALY gained if the daily cost of antiretroviral drugs is below $15 or if PrEP efficacy exceeds 75%. However, limitations include the lack of data on mixing patterns between lowand high-risk MSM. 17. Overall, PrEP can prevent a significant number of HIV infections, particularly in high-risk populations, but its high cost necessitates careful consideration of implementation strategies to ensure cost-effectiveness and sustainability.
